rationale: B wins by a slight margin because it sets harder proof gates before anyone starts pitching. Its line “from public product pages or the user's own verified research, not from Brex's sales deck” is the grown-up move; A's “A 50-country buildout tests what a $12.3B private fintech can afford” is interesting, but it can turn into a hostile finance story unless Brex has numbers it has not disclosed. B still has a made-up customer-story smell, but it labels the needed proof clearly enough to be useful.
gaps_in_A: “Geographic reach is a new front in a fight that has mostly been fought on features and pricing in the US” imports competitive history not supplied in the update. Verify it or cut it.

“issuing cards and running local reimbursement across Europe, Asia, and Latin America means dozens of regulatory and banking arrangements” turns likely plumbing complexity into stated fact. That needs sourcing.
“A 50-country buildout tests what a $12.3B private fintech can afford” is sharp but dangerous. “Afford” implies cost or burn pressure the update does not prove.

By refusing “A venture-backed startup scales its global team on Brex cards” outright, A loses the conditional customer workflow lane. With a named finance team, that may be the easiest trade placement.
gaps_in_B: “The finance team that stopped wiring reimbursements across borders” asserts a before-state not supplied in the facts.
“the wires, the FX losses, the month-end mess” is pain-point garnish until a real customer proves it.
“its biggest geographic move” is unsupported. The update gives “50 countries,” not Brex's expansion history.
B is right to reject “a bid to grow into its $12.3B valuation,” but it throws away the cleaner finance-scrutiny angle that the valuation and undisclosed profitability facts invite.
